initial_requirements: Project ZNIX aims to provide an object-based, application-independent framework for retrieving and manipulating personal information. Casual users should be able to archive diverse information, organize it through relationships and hierarchies they find meaningful, and add, change, remove, categorize, or back up items without disrupting that organization. The framework should also expose services that allow compatible client applications to work with the same information.

topics.topic_content: Editing, deleting, categorizing, and backing up stored items

slots.key: Supported item maintenance actions
slots.value: Add, change, remove, categorize, and back up items while keeping the item's structure intact; stability means relationships and hierarchy stay intact as items change over time. The storage model should be object-based, with archived information stored as discrete objects and relationships and metadata preserved rather than flattened into documents or rigid folders. From day one, essential capabilities also include archiving, retrieval, deletion, relationship management, and backup/restore, and the system should provide a service interface so compatible applications can access the same information without each maintaining its own separate copy. When a client can't support everything, it should still work safely with the subset it understands rather than corrupting or dropping shared information; limited clients can read and update what they support, but they shouldn't break the overall structure or hide missing features. Shared changes and backups should preserve authoritative data independently of any one application, and unsupported features should be preserved as data or metadata rather than lost.

slots.key: Behavior when an item is removed or replaced
slots.value: Items can be removed or replaced without forcing users to reorganize the remaining structure; users should be able to find the same item or related items reliably after additions, edits, deletions, or restore from backup, without rebuilding structure. If something is deleted, dependent references should be handled predictably, either by preserving them as broken references that can be repaired, or by applying a user-approved rule for that relationship. When dependent references can be repaired, ZNIX should repair them in a visible and traceable way so users know what changed; if they cannot be repaired, it should preserve enough information to flag the broken reference instead of silently discarding it. If a client only partially understands the references, it should leave the parts it does not understand untouched and pass them through safely, avoiding data loss and avoiding the appearance that the reference was fully resolved when it was not.

slots.key: Backup creation and restore expectations
slots.value: Backing up should preserve the user's chosen organization and structure so it stays intact when the information is restored or moved to another compatible tool; backups should bring the state back in a predictable way. Whatever storage format is used must support retrieval, organization, and backup without losing the user's structure or meaning. Shared changes and backups should preserve authoritative data in a way that is independent of any one application, so one weaker client doesn't become a point of failure; if a feature can't be represented in a given client, it should be preserved as data or metadata rather than lost. Backups should capture both the item and its context, including links and categories, so restoring an item brings back the meaning it had in the collection.

slots.key: Service ownership and handoff rules
slots.value: If a service becomes deprecated or unsupported, ZNIX should mark that status very clearly in the metadata that clients read so compatible apps can warn users before relying on it. Clients should also show a clear warning before use, ideally require user acknowledgment to continue, and limit creation of new dependencies such as new integrations or new data writes when a safer replacement exists. Higher-risk operations that could expose personal data more broadly, weaken permissions, or make recovery harder should be blocked immediately if the service is no longer trusted. Lower-risk read-only access may be allowed for a transition period only if it remains safe and is clearly marked as temporary. The acknowledgement should appear right before the client actually uses the service, not buried in settings, and the user can remember it per app and per service for a limited time. If the user declines, the client should not proceed with that service, especially for anything that writes or changes personal data; even for read-only or low-risk cases, declining should stop access unless the user explicitly chooses to continue.

topics.topic_content: Rules governing how personal information may be organized and altered

slots.key: Rules for preserving user-defined organization during edits
slots.value: Adding, changing, removing, categorizing, reusing across compatible tools, or backing up items should not disrupt the user's organization; the structure should stay intact when users edit, remove, or back things up. The relationships and hierarchy the user created should remain intact even when individual items change, links should not break or lose meaning just because content changes, and backups should be able to restore that state in a predictable way. Successful retrieval and updating also means users can find the right item quickly, update it without breaking its relationships, and trust that what they see afterward matches the information the system actually holds. Changes should feel immediate and consistent, especially when the same item is viewed through more than one client application. Avoid lost updates, broken links, stale displays, and confusing searches that return the wrong item or the right item only after too much effort. Delays are a problem if they interrupt normal work, but correctness matters more than making a fast wrong change. Relationships and metadata should stay intact as much as possible when an item changes, so updating the item doesn’t force users to rebuild the surrounding organization. Backups should capture both the item and its context, including links and categories, so restoring an item brings back the meaning it had in the collection. The main goal is to avoid silent loss of structure. The physical storage should preserve the object model rather than flattening everything into isolated records, keeping identifiers, relationships, and hierarchy separate from the content so retrieval and backup can reconstruct the same meaning. The storage format should be stable enough that objects can move, be renamed, or be reorganized without losing their links. If the same item appears in multiple contexts, the system should remember those relationships instead of treating it as three unrelated copies.

slots.value: The framework should be usable by casual users; it should be easy for everyday use, with reliability, data integrity, predictable behavior, and responsiveness so people can use it as part of their normal workflow.
